title: The Sword of the LORD Is Drawn
summary: God announces that he has drawn his sword against Jerusalem and the land, and Ezekiel is told to groan publicly at the coming news. A savage song celebrates the sharpened, polished sword. Then Ezekiel marks a fork in the road where the king of Babylon uses divination to choose between Ammon and Jerusalem; the lot falls on Jerusalem, the crown is removed from Judah's prince, and Ammon's turn comes after.
story: Chapter 20 ended with a riddle about fire in the southern forest, and the people complained that Ezekiel only spoke in parables. Chapter 21 drops the riddle. The fire is a sword, the forest is Jerusalem and its sanctuaries, and the agent of judgment is the king of Babylon. The chapter brings the book's warnings to a new pitch of urgency just a few years before the city fell. It also contains one of Ezekiel's rare glimpses of hope for the royal line: after the crown is removed and everything is left in ruins, it will be restored when the one comes to whom it rightly belongs (verse 27).
historical:
The chapter reflects the years around Zedekiah's revolt against Babylon, probably shortly before Nebuchadnezzar marched west in 589 or 588 BC. Zedekiah had been placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar and had sworn loyalty to him (2 Kings 24:17; Ezekiel 17:13-16), but he joined a coalition of small western states in rebellion. Jeremiah records envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon meeting in Jerusalem to discuss resistance (Jeremiah 27:3). That makes sense of the scene at the fork in the road: Ammon and Judah were both rebels, and Nebuchadnezzar had to decide which to strike first. He chose Jerusalem, which was besieged beginning in about January 588 BC and fell in 587 or 586 BC.

The Ammonites, whose capital Rabbah lies under modern Amman in Jordan, escaped for the moment. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century AD, reports that Nebuchadnezzar later campaigned against Ammon and Moab, some years after Jerusalem's fall. The prince called profane and wicked in verse 25 is Zedekiah, the last king of Judah.
cultural:
Verse 21 is a precise picture of Mesopotamian divination. Shaking arrows (belomancy) meant marking arrows with names, shaking them in a quiver, and drawing one out. Consulting the idols refers to teraphim, household images used in seeking omens. Examining the liver (hepatoscopy) was the most prestigious technique in Babylon: trained diviners inspected the liver of a sacrificed sheep, whose markings were believed to carry messages from the gods. Clay models of sheep livers, inscribed with omen interpretations for students, have been recovered from Mesopotamia and elsewhere in the ancient Near East. Ezekiel's point is pointed: the pagan king uses every pagan method, and the God of Israel guides the result.

The prophet's actions also belong to his world. Groaning publicly, striking the thigh, and clapping the hands were gestures of grief and alarm, and here they are performed as signs to provoke questions. The turban and crown of verse 26 are marks of royal office; the word for turban is used elsewhere for the high priest's headdress, and removing it means the end of Judah's rule.
literary: The chapter gathers four oracles, each opened by the word of the LORD. The first (verses 1 to 7) interprets the forest parable of 20:45-49 and commands the prophet's groaning. The second (verses 8 to 17) is the Song of the Sword, a fierce poem with short, repeated, almost chanted lines: a sword, a sword, sharpened and polished. Its Hebrew is notoriously difficult, especially verses 10 and 13, and translations differ considerably. The third (verses 18 to 27) is a sign-act, Ezekiel drawing a road map, followed by its interpretation and the oracle against Zedekiah, climaxing in the triple cry a ruin, a ruin. The fourth (verses 28 to 32) turns the sword on Ammon. Note that Hebrew Bibles number these verses 21:6-37, since 20:45-49 there begins chapter 21.

outline.t: God's sword drawn against Jerusalem and the land
The prophet groans at the coming news
The king of Babylon at the fork in the road
The profane prince uncrowned: a ruin until the rightful one comes

doctrines.note: A foreign king consults his gods at a crossroads, and the LORD directs the lot. The chapter shows God ruling over nations and events that know nothing of him, even using pagan divination to carry out his purpose.
The sword is the LORD's sword. Babylon's army is his instrument, and its coming is his judgment on a people who broke covenant and a king who broke his oath.
Verse 27 promises that the ruined royal rule will not be restored until the arrival of the one to whom it belongs. The line of David is cut down but not forgotten.

words.note: Cherev, sword. It appears fifteen times in the chapter, and the repetition is part of the message. The sword stands for war and the death it brings, and it is called God's own sword.

Qasam, to practice divination, to seek omens by technique. The Old Testament forbids it to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10) and consistently associates it with the nations and with false prophets. Here it is the Babylonian king's method, and in verse 29 the Ammonites' false visions.
Avvah, ruin or overthrow. It occurs three times in verse 27, the Hebrew way of expressing the superlative: complete ruin. The triple repetition is the lowest point of the chapter.
Anach, to sigh or groan. Ezekiel's groaning is itself a message. His body carries the grief the people should feel, and their question about it opens the door for the word.

christ: Verse 27 is the chapter's link to the larger story. The words until the arrival of him to whom it belongs are widely heard as an echo of Jacob's blessing of Judah, that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the one comes to whom it belongs, or until Shiloh comes (Genesis 49:10), a line translated in several ways. Ezekiel is saying that the kingship taken from Zedekiah is being held in trust for its rightful heir. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have read the line messianically, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David to whom God gives the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32-33). Verse 26 also sounds a note the New Testament will sing: the lowly exalted and the exalted brought low, which Mary proclaims in her song (Luke 1:52).

hard.q: How can God say his sword will cut off both the righteous and the wicked, when chapter 18 said each person answers for his own sin?
hard.a: The tension is real and sits within a few pages of the same book. Several responses are given. One is that the two chapters address different things. Chapter 18 concerns a person's standing before God, life or death in the sense of God's verdict, while chapter 21 describes the historical catastrophe of war, in which the innocent and guilty of a city suffer together. Another points out that the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, reads unrighteous and lawless in verse 3, suggesting that some ancient readers were uneasy with the Hebrew. A third reading hears the phrase as a way of saying everyone, without exception, much as English speaks of young and old. What the chapter does not say is that God regards the righteous and wicked alike in the end. The book elsewhere shows God marking the faithful who grieve over the city's sins (9:4) and preserving a remnant. War falls on all; God's final judgment does not treat all as the same.

questions: Ezekiel was told to groan in public so that people would ask why. What griefs over sin do you carry privately that might speak if they were seen?
The king of Babylon trusted arrows, idols, and livers, and God still steered the outcome. How does it comfort or unsettle you that God works even through people who do not know him?
Verse 26 says the lowly will be exalted and the exalted brought low. Where do you see that reversal at work, and where are you tempted to resist it?
